Time and Mutual Responsibility

Sample chapter 2. Research draft, 16 September 2026. Arabic and original English rendering require independent scholarly review before a reviewed edition.

A short text can be easy to remember and difficult to exhaust. Its few words may establish a situation, change our understanding of it, and leave us with something to do. But brevity alone proves little. A slogan can be brief. A proverb can be memorable. The question is what a composition achieves within its limits, and whether its different elements contribute to that achievement.

Surah al-ʿAṣr offers a manageable place to investigate. It comprises three verses. We can keep the entire composition in view while considering the relationships among its opening oath, its warning, and its exception. We need not begin by agreeing with the warning to understand how the language presents it.

Read the whole before explaining the parts

The following Arabic uses ordinary fully vowelled spelling, without reproducing all the specialized signs of a printed muṣḥaf. Its wording has been checked against the displayed text of Qur’an 103:1–3. ASR-001: Arabic text

وَالْعَصْرِ ۝١

إِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ لَفِي خُسْرٍ ۝٢

إِلَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ ۝٣

An original, deliberately transparent rendering:

By time,

indeed, the human being is surely in loss,

except those who believe, do righteous deeds, counsel one another to truth, and counsel one another to perseverance.

“Indeed” and “surely” make two Arabic emphatic elements visible, at the cost of somewhat heavier English. “The human being” preserves the singular grammatical form while inviting a generic reading. “Time” is an interpretive choice we will examine. “Perseverance” emphasizes endurance in ṣabr, although no single English equivalent reproduces every use of that word.

This rendering gives access to the argument. It cannot reproduce the Arabic sound pattern or settle every interpretive question. Those limitations are reasons to explain the choices, rather than to ask the reader to trust an unexplained assertion that translation loses everything important.

What does the oath bring into view?

The initial wa- is the particle of an oath: “By …” It is not simply the conjunction “and.” What follows is al-ʿaṣr. The construction directs attention toward something invoked in support of the statement that follows. The Quranic Arabic Corpus identifies the opening particle as an oath and the next verse’s lām as emphatic. These are grammatical observations, not judgments of literary superiority. ASR-002: morphological annotation

The meaning of ʿaṣr is not historically uncontested. Al-Ṭabarī reports temporal interpretations including time generally and a portion of the day. His own conclusion declines to restrict the oath to one meaning within its temporal range. Al-Zamakhsharī presents afternoon prayer, the later part of the day, and time as alternatives. We should not turn that plurality into the claim that all these meanings must be simultaneously intended. ASR-003: al-Ṭabarī on 103:1, ASR-004: al-Zamakhsharī on 103:1

On the reading “time,” the opening establishes a horizon within which human gain and loss become urgent. Whatever else a person possesses, a life unfolds through time. Read this way, the oath prepares us to hear “loss” as more than a passing disappointment. It raises the question of how a life is being spent.

That connection is an interpretation, not an additional word in the verse. The text does not explicitly say that every second is capital or that time itself proves the subsequent verdict. Those are ways of developing its imagery. A reader who prefers “afternoon” might instead hear the approach of a day’s ending. That reading can support a related meditation on limits, but it begins from a different lexical choice.

The literary proposal is therefore specific: under the broad temporal reading, the oath establishes a setting that gives the next statement greater existential reach. We can evaluate that proposal without declaring the other readings impossible.

A judgment made hard to overlook

The second verse contains inna, an emphatic particle, and the emphatic la- attached to fī. Its force exceeds an unmarked statement such as “people experience losses.” Al-Rāzī explicitly draws attention to both emphatic elements and to the expression “in loss,” which he interprets as suggesting surrounding or immersion. ASR-005: al-Rāzī on 103:2

Notice the difference between an event and a condition. Someone can lose an object while remaining otherwise secure. To be “in loss” presents loss as a condition within which the person stands. The preposition fī, “in,” makes that interpretation available. It does not require us to imagine a literal container.

Ibn ʿĀshūr similarly explains this spatial expression as figurative enclosure. He also treats the loss as a bad ultimate outcome, rather than merely unsuccessful commerce. Here the commercial contrast between loss and profit supplies an accessible way to speak about a life’s outcome. ASR-006: Ibn ʿĀshūr on 103:2

The subject, al-insān, is grammatically singular. Al-Ṭabarī explains why a plural exception can follow: the preceding expression has a collective sense. Al-Rāzī records both a generic interpretation and interpretations connecting the expression with particular opponents. Ibn ʿĀshūr qualifies the generality with reference to the people addressed by the emerging Islamic proclamation. The grammar makes a generic reading possible; it does not eliminate every dispute about the historical or theological scope. ASR-003: al-Ṭabarī on 103:3, ASR-005, ASR-006

Our working reading hears a judgment upon humanity, followed by an explicitly defined exception. Its rhetorical strength comes partly from that order. Before a listener learns who escapes the judgment, the statement has placed the human predicament before them in emphatic terms. Whether an individual listener actually feels alarm is an empirical question; the grammatical emphasis is available for inspection regardless.

The exception changes the composition

The third verse begins with illā, “except.” This small word prevents the preceding warning from becoming an account of unavoidable ruin. It also means that the positive description arrives as an answer to a problem already established.

The exception contains four coordinated predicates: believing, doing righteous deeds, mutually counseling truth, and mutually counseling perseverance. They describe the same plural group. The syntax does not present four unrelated routes from which a person chooses one.

Nor does coordination prove that the four descriptions have completely separate meanings. Mutual counsel can itself be a righteous deed. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the explicit mention of counsel after good action as giving particular attention to something included within the broader category. His reading warns against reducing good action to what a person does privately. ASR-006: Ibn ʿĀshūr on 103:3

This distinction matters for the book’s argument. A mechanical analysis might count four clauses and call the result four perfectly independent conditions. Close reading asks why partially overlapping descriptions have been given separate expression. Repetition and overlap can guide attention. They need not be defects, but their function must be demonstrated.

The first two predicates join conviction with conduct. The last two make relationships among people explicit. In tawāṣaw, the action is reciprocal: people counsel or exhort one another. Al-Ṭabarī explains it in precisely that interpersonal direction, with some advising others. The grammatical form is also recorded in the corpus as form VI. The contextual reading is supported by both sources; it should not be generalized into a rule that every form VI verb always has an identical reciprocal meaning. ASR-003, ASR-002

The effect is substantial. A paraphrase describing people who merely possess truth and patience would leave this relationship unexpressed. The verse describes participants in one another’s moral lives. A person can give counsel and also receive it. The wording makes mutual counsel explicit; it does not specify equal authority, equal participation, or an identical role for every member.

The two objects of counsel also need context. “Truth” should not quietly become whatever each participant happens to believe. Al-Ṭabarī connects it with God’s book and obedience to its teaching. Al-Zamakhsharī gives a broad religious interpretation encompassing monotheism, obedience, and adherence to revelation. These commentaries establish how their authors understood the verse; they do not independently prove the truth of the theology. ASR-003, ASR-004: al-Zamakhsharī on 103:3

Perseverance gives the final clause a different practical emphasis. Recognizing an obligation and sustaining it under difficulty are distinguishable tasks. In this reading, the ending supplies the endurance needed to continue the preceding commitments. The sequence moves from a warning about loss toward a form of shared life capable of persisting through time. That last connection is the present chapter’s interpretation of the whole, not a separate lexical definition.

Hear the arrangement, then test the explanation

At the customary verse-end stops, the endings ʿaṣr, khusr, and ṣabr share a final r. Their preceding sounds differ. Calling them three identical rhymes would conceal those differences. The repeated wa-tawāṣaw bi- in the last verse creates a more extensive parallel sequence. The two objects occupy corresponding positions in that sequence.

These observations let us ask a better question than “Does it sound beautiful?” Does the recurrence help a listener recognize the two acts of mutual counsel as related while keeping their objects distinct? That is a plausible functional explanation. Establishing an actual memory or comprehension advantage would require a study. No such result is reported here.

The whole composition can now be represented without numerical decoration:

Movement Textual basis Proposed contribution
Oath wa-l-ʿaṣr Establishes the temporal horizon under the reading used here.
Verdict Emphatic statement of being in loss Places the predicament before the listener.
Exception illā and the coordinated descriptions Identifies the community exempted from the verdict.
Closing parallel Repeated reciprocal verb and preposition Gives truth and perseverance distinct, corresponding attention.

The final column is interpretation. A diagram can make an argument easier to inspect, but cannot turn that interpretation into a measured fact.

Consider three original teaching paraphrases, not Qur’anic text and not translations:

Paraphrase Question it exposes
“People suffer losses, but good people do better.” What happens when emphatic judgment becomes a loose observation and the exception becomes vague?
“By time: humanity is in loss, except those who believe and do good.” What is left implicit when the mutual responsibilities are omitted?
“Those who believe, do good, and counsel one another to truth and perseverance escape loss. Others do not.” What changes when the positive group appears before the general verdict?

The first is deliberately thin. Defeating it establishes no superiority over accomplished human writing. The second exposes information that can be concealed by a compressed summary. The third retains much of the conceptual content but changes the order in which it arrives. A reader might reasonably find its directness useful for some purposes.

These alternatives help isolate choices. They do not prove that every conceivable alternative must be worse. A successful comparison must allow different wording and different techniques to accomplish comparable purposes.

What a fair comparison would require

A serious critic can accept this analysis and reply: human authors also use oaths, exceptions, emphasis, parallelism, and memorable endings. The observation is correct. Counting those devices cannot establish inimitability. The relevant question concerns their contribution within this composition, and then the strength of that contribution against carefully selected alternatives.

Another critic might find the passage’s abstract terms insufficiently specified. What beliefs? Which good deeds? Whose understanding of truth? The surrounding Qur’an and its interpretive traditions supply much of that context. The short surah can summarize a moral and theological orientation without being a self-contained explanation of every term. Its economy partly depends on that relationship. A comparison should give competing texts fair access to their own relevant contexts.

A third critic might accept its force while attributing that force to exceptional human authorship. Nothing established so far excludes that possibility. Religious familiarity may also affect a reader’s response. Repeated devotional exposure could help explain ease of recall or perceived solemnity. Those possibilities call for comparison and controls, not dismissal.

Before commissioning an evaluation, we would specify purposes broad enough to permit genuine alternatives: communicate a consequential judgment about human life, distinguish a response to it, and connect individual conduct with relationships among people. Then we would ask qualified readers to assess clarity, economy, coherence, and the contribution of sound, with reasons attached to each judgment. They must be allowed to reject the proposed criteria or explain why a comparator accomplishes something equally valuable differently.

Recognition cannot reliably be removed from a famous passage. Reviewers should therefore report familiarity and relevant commitments. The study should include strong short Arabic compositions nominated by readers who disagree about the Qur’an. Raters’ explanations and disagreements matter alongside any numerical summaries. No comparative superiority is established by the present chapter because that comparison has not yet been conducted.

A reader’s experiment

Choose one of the teaching paraphrases. Write down one meaning it preserves and one relationship it changes. Then identify whether your objection concerns missing content, order of presentation, sound, or personal preference. If you think it improves something, specify the improvement.

Next, return to the Arabic and the transparent rendering. Separate three statements: “the reciprocal expression occurs twice”; “its repetition gives the two responsibilities corresponding prominence”; and “this is exceptionally accomplished writing.” The first is directly checkable. The second requires an argument about function. The third requires evaluative judgment and meaningful comparison.

The theological claim asks for a further step. This chapter contributes an inspectable example of how a small composition coordinates warning, exception, conviction, action, and mutual responsibility. If comparable achievements prove substantial and sustained across the text, they belong in a cumulative argument about its origin. Establishing that larger case requires evidence beyond these three verses.

Al-ʿAṣr leaves us with more than an isolated verbal flourish. On the reading developed here, its opening places human life within time; its middle confronts that life with loss; its ending describes people sustaining commitments with one another. The reader can now examine that relationship, challenge its interpretation, and ask what would count as a comparable achievement. That is a firmer beginning for the inimitability argument than asking admiration to perform the work of evidence.

Source and review note

The linked sources were inspected on 16 September 2026. ASR-001 is the Arabic text; ASR-002 is a modern annotation resource; ASR-003 through ASR-005 reproduce classical commentaries; ASR-006 reproduces Ibn ʿĀshūr’s modern commentary. These are six works/resources, not six independent confirmations of every interpretation. Tafsir authors share textual and interpretive traditions.
